concept: Pipeline RAG (end-to-end retrieval-augmented generation: routing, retrieval, compression, generation, grounding, evaluation)
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation began as a trained architecture that pairs a parametric generator with a non-parametric index (Lewis et al. 2020, NeurIPS; REALM, Guu et al. 2020; RETRO, Borgeaud et al. 2022), then shifted toward "black-box" augmentation in which retrieved text is simply prepended to a frozen LLM's prompt and only the retriever or a light adapter is tuned (REPLUG: +6.3% LM for GPT-3 175B, +5.1% MMLU for Codex; RA-DIT: up to +8.9% zero-shot). The state of the art in 2024-2026 is no longer a linear retrieve-then-read chain but a modular, conditional, branching and looping graph (Gao et al. 2023 survey; Gao et al. 2024 "Modular RAG"): a router decides whether and how to retrieve (Adaptive-RAG: a 770M-parameter classifier picks no/single/multi-step retrieval and matches multi-step accuracy at ~40% of its latency; Self-Route: routes 57-82% of queries to cheap RAG and falls back to long-context, cutting tokens 39-65% at near-long-context quality); query transformers reshape the request (Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, HyDE, Step-Back: +7 to +27 points on PaLM-2L); hybrid lexical+dense retrieval with contextualized chunks and a reranking cascade reduces top-20 retrieval failures by 67% (Anthropic Contextual Retrieval); hierarchical or graph indexes answer document-level and corpus-level questions that chunk retrieval cannot (RAPTOR: +20 absolute on QuALITY; GraphRAG: 72-83% win rate on comprehensiveness vs vector RAG); a corrective/self-reflective gate judges retrieved evidence before generation (CRAG, Self-RAG reflection tokens); compression keeps only 5-10% of retrieved tokens with at most ~10% relative loss (RECOMP) or 2-6x fewer tokens with +21.4% accuracy on NQ (LongLLMLingua); and generation is citation-grounded and checked by NLI-based citation precision/recall (ALCE) plus reference-free triad metrics (RAGAS faithfulness/answer relevance/context relevance; ARES fine-tuned judges with prediction-powered inference).

Two empirical facts dominate production design. First, position effects are real: GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 documents scores 75.8% when the gold passage is first, 53.8% when it is tenth (below the 56.1% closed-book baseline), and reader performance saturates near k=20 even as retriever recall keeps rising (Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle"). Second, RAG systems fail at predictable seams (Barnett et al.'s seven failure points: missing content, missed top-ranked docs, not in context, not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, incomplete) and "validation is only feasible during operation," so observability and continuous evaluation are first-class components rather than afterthoughts. Long-context models have not displaced RAG: when resources allow, long context wins on average (Li et al. 2024), but retrieval still improves even 32K-context models (Xu et al., ICLR 2024) and is far cheaper, so the production answer is a hybrid router, not either/or. The agentic turn (Singh et al. 2025) wraps all of this in planning, reflection and tool-use loops, which is the natural shape for a task-agnostic, prompt-driven pipeline component.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
papers.authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktäschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela
papers.citation_signal: Origin of the term 'RAG'; NeurIPS 2020; the most-cited paper in the field and the reference point every later RAG paper cites (Meta AI).
papers.key_contribution: Combines a pre-trained seq2seq generator (parametric memory) with a DPR dense index over Wikipedia (non-parametric memory), end-to-end fine-tuned. Two variants: RAG-Sequence (same passages for the whole output) and RAG-Token (different passages per token). Set state of the art on three open-domain QA tasks and produced more specific, diverse and factual generations than parametric-only baselines.
papers.design_implication: Establishes the separable retriever/generator contract: the index can be swapped or refreshed without retraining the generator. A production component should treat the index as hot-swappable non-parametric memory with its own versioning, and should expose per-passage marginalization (RAG-Sequence vs RAG-Token) conceptually as 'fuse evidence across passages' rather than relying on a single top hit.

papers.title: REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training
papers.authors: Kelvin Guu, Kenton Lee, Zora Tung, Panupong Pasupat, Ming-Wei Chang
papers.citation_signal: Foundational Google paper; thousands of citations; first to backpropagate through retrieval over millions of documents during pre-training.
papers.key_contribution: Adds a latent knowledge retriever trained unsupervised via masked-LM signal, backpropagating through retrieval over millions of Wikipedia documents. On three open-domain QA benchmarks it beats prior explicit and implicit knowledge-storage methods by 4-16% absolute accuracy, with interpretability and modularity benefits.
papers.design_implication: Shows that the retriever can be trained from downstream usefulness signals rather than relevance labels. In production, log which retrieved chunks actually contributed to accepted answers and use that signal to fine-tune or re-weight the retriever (the same idea REPLUG and RA-DIT later made black-box compatible). Also motivates asynchronous index refresh: REALM re-embeds the corpus periodically while training continues.

papers.title: Improving language models by retrieving from trillions of tokens (RETRO)
papers.authors: Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Jordan Hoffmann, et al. (28 authors, DeepMind)
papers.citation_signal: DeepMind; ICML 2022; widely cited as proof that retrieval substitutes for parameters at scale.
papers.key_contribution: Conditions an autoregressive LM on chunks retrieved from a 2-trillion-token database by local similarity to preceding tokens, via a frozen BERT retriever and chunked cross-attention. RETRO matches GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile with 25x fewer parameters; gains transfer to QA after fine-tuning; existing transformers can be 'RETROfitted'.
papers.design_implication: Retrieval is a compute/parameter trade: a smaller model plus a large, cheap index can match a much larger model. For a company pipeline this argues for routing routine, knowledge-heavy queries to a smaller retrieval-augmented model and reserving frontier models for reasoning-heavy steps. Chunk-level (not document-level) retrieval keyed on the running context is the origin of the sliding-window/active-retrieval pattern.

papers.title: REPLUG: Retrieval-Augmented Black-Box Language Models
papers.authors: Weijia Shi, Sewon Min, Michihiro Yasunaga, Minjoon Seo, Rich James, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Wen-tau Yih
papers.citation_signal: Hundreds of citations; the canonical justification for prepend-only RAG with API-hosted LLMs.
papers.key_contribution: Treats the LLM as a black box; retrieved documents are prepended to the input and the LM's output likelihoods supervise the retriever (REPLUG LSR). The tuned retriever improves GPT-3 175B language modeling by 6.3% and Codex five-shot MMLU by 5.1%. Multiple retrieved documents are processed in parallel and their next-token distributions ensembled.
papers.design_implication: Validates the production reality that the generator is an API you cannot modify. The retriever is the tunable part; collect LM feedback (answer acceptance, judge scores) as training signal. The parallel-ensemble trick maps directly onto a parallelization component: fan out k independent generations over k evidence sets and aggregate.

papers.title: RA-DIT: Retrieval-Augmented Dual Instruction Tuning
papers.authors: Xi Victoria Lin, Xilun Chen, Mingda Chen, Weijia Shi, Maria Lomeli, Rich James, Pedro Rodriguez, Jacob Kahn, Gergely Szilvasy, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Scott Yih
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 (Meta FAIR); reference method for lightweight retrieval fine-tuning.
papers.key_contribution: Two-step lightweight fine-tuning: (1) tune the LM to better use retrieved text (and to ignore irrelevant text), (2) tune the retriever toward documents the LM prefers. RA-DIT 65B sets SOTA on knowledge-intensive zero/few-shot benchmarks, beating in-context RALM approaches by up to +8.9% (0-shot) and +1.4% (5-shot).
papers.design_implication: If the company hosts an open-weight model, a modest dual-tuning pass on in-domain (code, spec, incident) data yields the largest gains and teaches the model to disregard noisy retrievals, which is the cheapest mitigation for Barnett's FP4 (not extracted). Even when fine-tuning is impossible, the lesson applies to prompt design: instruct the model explicitly that retrieved context may be irrelevant and should be ignored when so.

papers.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
papers.authors: Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 oral; Paper Digest ranks it the #6 most influential ICLR 2024 paper; >1,000 citations; reference design for reflective RAG.
papers.key_contribution: Trains one LM to emit reflection tokens: Retrieve {yes,no,continue}, IsRel {relevant,irrelevant}, IsSup {fully,partially,no support}, IsUse {1-5}. Inference uses segment-level beam search (width 2) scored by generation probability plus a weighted critique score (default weights IsRel 1.0, IsSup 1.0, IsUse 0.5); retrieval triggers when P(Retrieve=yes) > 0.2 (0 for citation tasks). Self-RAG 7B/13B: PopQA 54.9/55.8 vs ChatGPT 29.3; PubHealth 72.4/74.5 vs 70.1; Bio FactScore 81.2/80.2 vs 71.8; ASQA citation precision 66.9/70.3 and recall 67.8/71.3.
papers.design_implication: Externalize the four reflection decisions as explicit, logged pipeline stages (retrieve?, relevant?, supported?, useful?) implemented either by a trained small model or by LLM-judge prompts. Expose the critique weights and the retrieval threshold as runtime configuration so the same component can be tuned for high-precision engineering domains (raise IsSup weight, use hard filter on 'no support') versus exploratory ones.

papers.title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG)
papers.authors: Shi-Qi Yan, Jia-Chen Gu, Yun Zhu, Zhen-Hua Ling
papers.citation_signal: Hundreds of citations; implemented as an official LangGraph/LangChain tutorial pattern and widely re-implemented in industry.
papers.key_contribution: A lightweight retrieval evaluator (T5-large, ~0.77B) scores each retrieved document in [-1,1]; thresholds map to Correct (refine via decompose-then-recompose knowledge strips), Incorrect (discard and fall back to web search), or Ambiguous (do both). Thresholds set empirically per dataset, e.g. PopQA (0.59, -0.99), Biography (0.95, -0.91), PubHealth/ARC (0.5, -0.91). With LLaMA2-7B: PopQA 50.5 -> 54.9, PubHealth 48.9 -> 59.5, ARC 43.4 -> 53.7 over RAG; Self-CRAG on SelfRAG-7B: PopQA 61.8, Biography FactScore 86.2.
papers.design_implication: Implement a plug-in 'evidence gate' with a three-way confidence decision and a configurable fallback retriever (web, secondary corpus, or escalate to human). Calibrate the two thresholds per domain on a small labeled set; do not hard-code the paper's values. The decompose-then-recompose step (split retrieved docs into strips, score, keep relevant strips) is an inexpensive extractive compressor that composes with RECOMP-style compression.

papers.title: Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
papers.authors: Soyeong Jeong, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park
papers.citation_signal: NAACL 2024; the standard citation for complexity-based RAG routing; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: A T5-large (770M) classifier trained on automatically derived labels routes queries to (A) no retrieval, (B) single-step retrieval, or (C) multi-step IRCoT-style retrieval. Label distribution: 8.6% A, 53.3% B, 38.1% C. With GPT-3.5: Adaptive-RAG F1 50.91 / acc 48.97 at 1.03 retrieval steps and 1.46x single-step time, vs multi-step 50.87 / 49.70 at 2.81 steps and 3.33x time. Smaller classifiers (60M, 223M) were within ~1 F1 of the large one.
papers.design_implication: Front the pipeline with a cheap complexity router (a 60M-770M classifier or a one-token LLM call) that selects among at least three execution plans; this is where most of the latency/cost savings come from. Train or calibrate the router on production traces (which plan succeeded cheapest) rather than static labels, and log plan choice as a metric for drift detection.

papers.title: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation (FLARE)
papers.authors: Zhengbao Jiang, Frank F. Xu, Luyu Gao, Zhiqing Sun, Qian Liu, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Yiming Yang, Jamie Callan, Graham Neubig
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 (CMU); hundreds of citations; canonical 'when to retrieve during generation' method.
papers.key_contribution: Generates a tentative next sentence, and if it contains tokens below a confidence threshold, uses that sentence (masked or as generated questions) as a retrieval query and regenerates the sentence with retrieved evidence. Superior or competitive on four long-form knowledge-intensive tasks (multihop QA, commonsense reasoning, long-form QA, open-domain summarization) versus single-time and fixed-interval retrieval.
papers.design_implication: For long-form outputs (design documents, incident postmortems, requirement summaries), schedule retrieval per section/sentence driven by model confidence (token logprobs where available, or a self-rated confidence otherwise) rather than once up front. Expose the confidence threshold and maximum retrieval calls per response as configuration to bound latency.

papers.title: Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions (IRCoT)
papers.authors: Harsh Trivedi, Niranjan Balasubramanian, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal
papers.citation_signal: ACL 2023 (AI2); the baseline multi-step retrieval method reused by Adaptive-RAG and many others.
papers.key_contribution: Alternates one chain-of-thought sentence with one retrieval step, using the latest CoT sentence as the query and appending retrieved paragraphs to the context. With GPT-3 it improves retrieval recall by up to 21 points and downstream QA by up to 15 points on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and IIRC; gains hold out-of-distribution and with Flan-T5-large; reduces hallucination.
papers.design_implication: The multi-step plan in a router should be IRCoT-shaped: reason one step, retrieve with the reasoning as the query, repeat, with a hard cap on steps (Adaptive-RAG's multi-step averaged 2.1-4.7 steps). This is the natural integration point with a task-decomposition component: each sub-question becomes one retrieve-and-reason iteration.

papers.title: RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval
papers.authors: Parth Sarthi, Salman Abdullah, Aditi Tuli, Shubh Khanna, Anna Goldie, Christopher D. Manning
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 (Stanford, Manning); hundreds of citations; implemented in LlamaIndex and LangChain.
papers.key_contribution: Splits text into ~100-token chunks, embeds, clusters with UMAP + Gaussian mixture models (BIC selects cluster count, soft assignment), summarizes each cluster with gpt-3.5-turbo and recurses to build a tree. Querying by 'collapsed tree' (all nodes flattened, top nodes within a 2,000-token budget, about top-20) beat tree traversal. RAPTOR + GPT-4: QuALITY 82.6% (prior best 62.3%), QASPER 55.7 F1 (CoLT5 XL 53.9), NarrativeQA new SOTA on METEOR.
papers.design_implication: Index at multiple abstraction levels so that both detail questions and 'what does this spec/document say overall' questions are answerable; store summary nodes in the same vector index with a level tag and retrieve with a token budget rather than a fixed k. For engineering corpora the tree aligns with document structure (section -> chapter -> document), so structure-aware clustering can replace or seed GMM clustering.

papers.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
papers.authors: Darren Edge, Ha Trinh, Newman Cheng, Joshua Bradley, Alex Chao, Apurva Mody, Steven Truitt, Dasha Metropolitansky, Robert Osazuwa Ness, Jonathan Larson
papers.citation_signal: Microsoft Research; open-source repo with 20K-33K+ GitHub stars and enterprise adoption; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: Builds an entity knowledge graph with LLM extraction over 600-token chunks (100-token overlap), uses 'gleaning' prompts to recover missed entities, partitions with Leiden into hierarchical communities (C0 root to C3 leaf), pre-summarizes communities, and answers global questions by map-reduce over community summaries. On ~1M-token podcast and ~1.7M-token news corpora, community summaries beat vector RAG with 72-83% win rate on comprehensiveness and 62-82% on diversity (p<.001); root-level C0 still wins 72%/62% while using 9-43x fewer context tokens than source-text map-reduce.
papers.design_implication: Add a 'global question' plan to the router: corpus-level sensemaking (themes across incident reports, cross-cutting requirements) should hit pre-computed community summaries, not chunk search. Choose the community level by budget (C0 for cheap overviews, C2/C3 for detail). Indexing cost is high (many LLM calls), so build graphs incrementally and only for corpora where global questions are expected.

papers.title: Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
papers.authors: Xinbei Ma, Yeyun Gong, Pengcheng He, Hai Zhao, Nan Duan
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 (Microsoft Research Asia); the standard citation for Rewrite-Retrieve-Read; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: Replaces retrieve-then-read with Rewrite-Retrieve-Read: an LLM (or a small trainable T5 rewriter) rewrites the user query into search-engine-friendly queries before retrieval; the small rewriter is trained with reinforcement learning from the frozen reader's downstream reward. Consistent gains on open-domain QA (HotpotQA, AmbigNQ, PopQA) and multiple-choice QA (MMLU) with a frozen ChatGPT reader.
papers.design_implication: Decouple the user's natural-language task prompt from the retrieval query. A dedicated rewrite stage (one cheap LLM call or a distilled small model) should emit one or more retrieval queries with a declared intent; keep the stage replaceable so a trained rewriter can be swapped in once production reward signals exist.

papers.title: Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Swaroop Mishra, Xinyun Chen, Heng-Tze Cheng, Ed H. Chi, Quoc V Le, Denny Zhou
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 (Google DeepMind); hundreds of citations; widely adopted as a query-transformation technique in RAG frameworks.
papers.key_contribution: Prompts the model to first abstract the specific question to a higher-level concept or principle (the 'step-back question'), retrieve/reason about that, then answer the original. On PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics +7%, Chemistry +11%, TimeQA +27%, MuSiQue +7%; also tested on GPT-4 and Llama2-70B.
papers.design_implication: Include step-back abstraction as one of the query variants in a multi-query fan-out: retrieve for both the literal question and its abstracted principle (e.g. for 'why did relay K12 fail at 85 C', also retrieve the relay's derating standard). Especially valuable for engineering questions whose answer lives in a general standard rather than the specific incident record.

papers.title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)
papers.authors: Luyu Gao, Xueguang Ma, Jimmy Lin, Jamie Callan
papers.citation_signal: ACL 2023; implemented in LangChain and LlamaIndex; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: An instruction-following LLM writes a hypothetical answer document for the query; an unsupervised contrastive encoder (Contriever) embeds it and retrieves real documents near it. The embedding bottleneck filters hallucinated detail. Significantly outperforms Contriever zero-shot and is comparable to fine-tuned retrievers across web search, QA, fact verification and non-English languages.
papers.design_implication: Use HyDE as an opt-in query transform when the embedding model is generic and the domain vocabulary differs from user phrasing (e.g. users ask in plain English, documents are formal specs). Disable it when the LLM is unlikely to know the domain (private part numbers), because the hypothetical document will then be noise; a router flag or confidence check should decide.

papers.title: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Huiqiang Jiang, Qianhui Wu, Chin-Yew Lin, Yuqing Yang, Lili Qiu
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 (Microsoft); open-source library with broad adoption (LlamaIndex/LangChain integrations).
papers.key_contribution: Coarse-to-fine prompt compression using a small LM's perplexity: a budget controller allocates compression across demonstrations/instructions/question, token-level iterative compression drops low-information tokens, and instruction tuning aligns the small LM's distribution to the target LLM. Up to 20x compression with little performance loss on GSM8K, BBH, ShareGPT and Arxiv-March23.
papers.design_implication: Deploy a compression stage between retrieval and generation with a configurable token budget; apply aggressive ratios to few-shot demonstrations and moderate ratios to retrieved evidence. Keep an escape hatch for code, identifiers and numeric tables where token dropping is destructive.

papers.title: LongLLMLingua: Accelerating and Enhancing LLMs in Long Context Scenarios via Prompt Compression
papers.authors: Huiqiang Jiang, Qianhui Wu, Xufang Luo, Dongsheng Li, Chin-Yew Lin, Yuqing Yang, Lili Qiu
papers.citation_signal: ACL 2024 (Microsoft); the RAG-specific successor to LLMLingua; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: Question-aware coarse-grained (document-level) and fine-grained (token-level) compression plus document reordering to counter position bias. On NaturalQuestions with GPT-3.5-Turbo: up to +21.4% accuracy with ~4x fewer tokens; 94.0% cost reduction on LooGLE; 1.4x-2.6x end-to-end latency speedup at 2x-6x compression on ~10k-token prompts.
papers.design_implication: Compression and reordering together both cut cost and raise accuracy, so they should be the default, not an optimization. Implement question-aware document scoring, reorder so the highest-scored documents sit at the start (and end) of the context, then compress within a budget.

papers.title: RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Context Compression and Selective Augmentation
papers.authors: Fangyuan Xu, Weijia Shi, Eunsol Choi
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 (UT Austin / UW); the reference for selective augmentation; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: Two trained compressors: extractive (Contriever-initialized dual encoder, ~110M, picks top 1-2 sentences) and abstractive (T5-large, 775M, distilled from GPT-3.5 summaries filtered by end-task gain). With Flan-UL2 20B, top-5 documents (660-684 tokens) compress to 32-75 tokens: NQ EM 39.39 -> 37.04, TriviaQA 62.37 -> 58.68, HotpotQA 32.80 -> 30.40 (extractive). Compression to 5-10% of tokens with at most ~10% relative loss; abstractive compressor outputs an empty string for 4-25% of training examples where retrieval hurt (selective augmentation).
papers.design_implication: Train or prompt the compressor to return nothing when evidence is unhelpful; this directly implements the 'no retrieval' branch at a stage that already sees the documents. Prefer extractive compression for multi-hop or precision-critical domains (code, specs) and abstractive compression for narrative sources (incident reports, meeting notes).

papers.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
papers.authors: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang
papers.citation_signal: TACL (Stanford); >2,000 citations; coined the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon referenced across RAG and long-context work.
papers.key_contribution: Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval show a U-shaped curve: GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 documents scores 75.8% with the gold document first, 53.8% at position 10 (below the 56.1% closed-book baseline) and 63.2% at position 20. Performance also degrades as context grows, even for long-context models. Reader performance saturates long before retriever recall: beyond 20 retrieved documents GPT-3.5 gains ~1.5% and Claude-1.3 ~1%.
papers.design_implication: Rerank and then order evidence so the most relevant chunks occupy the beginning and end of the context; cap evidence at roughly 10-20 chunks for chat-sized models; prefer compression over longer contexts. Treat 'more context' as a cost with diminishing or negative return, and measure position sensitivity on your own model in evaluation.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.authors: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan, Yuxi Bi, Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun, Meng Wang, Haofen Wang
papers.citation_signal: The most-cited RAG survey (thousands of citations); defines the Naive/Advanced/Modular RAG taxonomy used across industry.
papers.key_contribution: Organizes RAG into Naive, Advanced and Modular paradigms and into retrieval, generation and augmentation components; catalogs pre-retrieval (query rewriting, routing, expansion), retrieval (chunking, embedding fine-tuning, hybrid) and post-retrieval (reranking, compression) optimizations; summarizes evaluation frameworks and open problems.
papers.design_implication: Use its taxonomy as the component's module boundary: pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, generation, each with swappable operators. The 'Advanced RAG' checklist (rewrite, hybrid search, rerank, compress) should be the baseline configuration a production system ships with.

papers.title: Modular RAG: Transforming RAG Systems into LEGO-like Reconfigurable Frameworks
papers.authors: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Meng Wang, Haofen Wang
papers.citation_signal: Follow-up by the authors of the dominant RAG survey; widely referenced as the architectural vocabulary for RAG orchestration frameworks.
papers.key_contribution: Decomposes RAG into modules and operators and identifies four RAG flow patterns (linear, conditional, branching, looping) with routing, scheduling and fusion mechanisms, mapping existing methods (Self-RAG, FLARE, IRCoT, etc.) onto them and proposing a roadmap of future operators.
papers.design_implication: Implement the pipeline as a typed graph with these four control-flow primitives: linear chains, conditional edges (routers), parallel branches with a fusion node, and bounded loops. Every published RAG method then becomes a configuration (a sub-graph) rather than new code, which is what 'task-agnostic and tweakable' requires.

papers.title: Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System
papers.authors: Scott Barnett, Stefanus Kurniawan, Srikanth Thudumu, Zach Brannelly, Mohamed Abdelrazek
papers.venue: CAIN 2024 (3rd International Conference on AI Engineering, co-located with ICSE), IEEE
papers.citation_signal: CAIN/ICSE 2024 (Deakin University); the standard engineering failure taxonomy cited in RAG practice guides and tooling docs.
papers.key_contribution: Experience report from three case studies (research, education, biomedical). Seven failure points: FP1 Missing Content, FP2 Missed Top Ranked Documents, FP3 Not in Context (lost in consolidation), FP4 Not Extracted, FP5 Wrong Format, FP6 Incorrect Specificity, FP7 Incomplete. Lessons: chunking quality drives everything, re-embedding on strategy change is costly, open-source embeddings matched closed ones on small text, test data is scarce, and 'validation of a RAG system is only feasible during operation'.
papers.design_implication: Map every observability metric to a failure point: abstention rate (FP1), gold-in-top-k (FP2), gold-in-context after consolidation (FP3), faithfulness/answer-in-context-but-missed (FP4), schema validation failures (FP5), specificity judge (FP6), completeness judge (FP7). Build continuous evaluation on live traffic with sampling and human review rather than relying on an offline benchmark alone.

papers.title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Shahul Es, Jithin James, Luis Espinosa-Anke, Steven Schockaert
papers.citation_signal: EACL 2024 demo; the ragas library is the most widely adopted open-source RAG evaluation toolkit; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: Reference-free metrics: faithfulness (decompose answer into statements, fraction supported by context), answer relevance (generate questions from the answer, mean cosine similarity to the original question), context relevance (fraction of context sentences needed for the answer). On WikiEval (50 pages, human-annotated), pairwise agreement with humans: 0.95 faithfulness, 0.78 answer relevance, 0.70 context relevance, vs GPT Score 0.72/0.52/0.63 and GPT Ranking 0.54/0.40/0.52.
papers.design_implication: Instrument the pipeline with the RAGAS triad on sampled live traffic as the default health signal; faithfulness is reliable enough to gate releases, context relevance is the weakest and should be complemented by retrieval recall measured against labeled sets. Treat RAGAS scores as relative (A/B between pipeline configs), not absolute quality.

papers.title: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
papers.authors: Jon Saad-Falcon, Omar Khattab, Christopher Potts, Matei Zaharia
papers.citation_signal: NAACL 2024 (Stanford/Databricks); reference method for statistically calibrated RAG evaluation.
papers.key_contribution: Generates synthetic queries/answers with FLAN-T5 XXL (plus weak and strong negatives), fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-large judges for context relevance, answer faithfulness and answer relevance, then applies prediction-powered inference with ~150 human-annotated points to produce 95% confidence intervals. Kendall tau on real systems 0.91 (context relevance) and 0.97 (answer relevance), 0.16 and 0.15 above RAGAS; robust to domain shift in query/document type across eight KILT/SuperGLUE/AIS tasks.
papers.design_implication: For a company pipeline, invest in a small (150-300) human-labeled validation set per domain and use it to calibrate LLM or small-model judges with PPI; this turns noisy judge scores into confidence intervals suitable for release decisions. Synthetic in-domain QA generation (with hard negatives) is the practical way to get evaluation data for engineering corpora.

papers.title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
papers.authors: Tianyu Gao, Howard Yen, Jiatong Yu, Danqi Chen
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 (Princeton); the standard citation benchmark used by Self-RAG and later attribution work; hundreds of citations.
papers.key_contribution: Benchmark over ASQA, QAMPARI and ELI5 with automatic fluency, correctness and citation metrics. Citation recall = fraction of statements entailed by their cited passages; citation precision = fraction of citations that are individually necessary, judged by the TRUE NLI model (T5-11B). Top-5 passages is the main setting; for ChatGPT correctness plateaus at top-1 and citation quality at top-3, while GPT-4 keeps improving up to 20 passages. Summaries (SUMM) raise correctness (40.4 -> 43.3) but lower citation recall (73.6 -> 68.9). Even the best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time on ELI5; retrieval quality is a major bottleneck.
papers.design_implication: Make per-statement citations a hard output contract and verify them with an NLI/judge model before returning; expose citation precision/recall as release metrics. Because compression trades citation recall for correctness, keep a pointer from each compressed snippet back to its source span so citations resolve to original text.

papers.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach (Self-Route)
papers.authors: Zhuowan Li, Cheng Li, Mingyang Zhang, Qiaozhu Mei, Michael Bendersky
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2024 industry track (Google DeepMind); the most-cited RAG-vs-long-context study.
papers.key_contribution: Across LongBench and InfiniteBench datasets with Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT-4O and GPT-3.5-Turbo, long context (LC) beats RAG (300-word chunks, k=5, Contriever or Dragon) on average: 49.70 vs 37.33 (Gemini), 48.67 vs 32.60 (GPT-4O). Self-Route first answers with RAG and lets the model declare 'unanswerable', then falls back to LC: 57-82% of queries stay on RAG, token cost drops 65% (Gemini) and 39% (GPT-4O) with scores 46.41 / 48.89 / 35.32 (within -2.2% to +1.7% of LC). RAG failures cluster into multi-step reasoning, general queries, long/complex queries and implicit whole-context queries.
papers.design_implication: Implement a two-tier execution: cheap RAG with an explicit abstention option, then escalate to long-context (whole document or RAPTOR/GraphRAG summaries) on abstention. The four RAG failure categories are the labels your router should learn to detect up front so escalation happens before wasted calls.

papers.title: Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models
papers.authors: Peng Xu, Wei Ping, Xianchao Wu, Lawrence McAfee, Chen Zhu, Zihan Liu, Sandeep Subramanian, Evelina Bakhturina, Mohammad Shoeybi, Bryan Catanzaro
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 (NVIDIA); widely cited counterpoint showing retrieval helps even with long context.
papers.key_contribution: A 4K-context LLM with simple retrieval augmentation matches a 16K-context model fine-tuned via positional interpolation on long-context tasks at far lower compute. Retrieval improves performance regardless of context window; retrieval-augmented Llama2-70B-32K beats GPT-3.5-turbo-16k and Davinci003 on average over nine long-context tasks (QA, query-based summarization, in-context few-shot) and outperforms its non-retrieval counterpart while generating faster.
papers.design_implication: Do not drop retrieval when adopting long-context models; retrieval narrows the context to relevant spans, improving both quality and latency. The combination 'long window + retrieval of top chunks' is the safe default for engineering documents that exceed a few hundred pages.

papers.title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
papers.authors: Aditi Singh, Abul Ehtesham, Saket Kumar, Tala Talaei Khoei, Athanasios V. Vasilakos
papers.citation_signal: Widely cited 2025 survey (hundreds of citations) defining the agentic RAG taxonomy used by practitioners.
papers.key_contribution: Surveys architectures that embed autonomous agents (reflection, planning, tool use, multi-agent collaboration) into RAG; proposes a taxonomy by agent cardinality, control structure, autonomy and knowledge representation; compares single-agent, multi-agent, hierarchical, corrective, adaptive and graph-based agentic RAG; reviews applications (healthcare, finance, education, enterprise documents) and open challenges in evaluation, coordination, memory, efficiency and governance.
papers.design_implication: A task-agnostic component that 'accepts a prompt and reasons about how to execute it' is by definition agentic RAG: a planner agent should select and sequence the retrieval operators (routing, rewriting, hybrid search, graph lookup, compression, verification) as tools. Bound autonomy with step budgets, deterministic fallbacks and audit logs, which the survey lists as the main governance gap.

papers.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods
papers.authors: Gordon V. Cormack, Charles L. A. Clarke, Stefan Büttcher
papers.citation_signal: SIGIR 2009; the default fusion method in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Weaviate, Azure AI Search and most hybrid RAG stacks.
papers.key_contribution: Fuses ranked lists by score(d) = sum over rankers of 1/(k + rank(d)), with k=60 fixed in a pilot and never re-tuned; RRF consistently equaled or beat Condorcet Fuse and CombMNZ on TREC runs and built a LETOR 3 meta-learner better than previously reported methods.
papers.design_implication: Use RRF with k=60 as the default to merge BM25, dense and any additional retrievers (HyDE, multi-query variants) before reranking; it needs no score normalization and is robust to heterogeneous scorers. Expose k and per-retriever weights as configuration but ship with the literature default.

papers.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
papers.authors: Anthropic (engineering blog)
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative vendor engineering guidance; widely adopted ('contextual chunking') across RAG frameworks and reproduced by independent benchmarks.
papers.key_contribution: Prepends an LLM-generated 50-100-token context to each chunk before embedding and before building the BM25 index. Measured as top-20 retrieval failure rate: baseline 5.7%, contextual embeddings 3.7% (-35%), contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 2.9% (-49%), plus reranking 1.9% (-67%). Pipeline: retrieve top-150, rerank (Cohere), keep top-20 (top-20 beat top-10 and top-5). One-time indexing cost about $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching. Recommends skipping RAG when the knowledge base is under ~200K tokens (~500 pages) and using prompt caching (>2x latency, up to 90% cost reduction).
papers.design_implication: Ship contextual chunking + hybrid BM25/dense + rerank cascade (150 -> 20) as the default retrieval configuration; it is the best-documented production recipe. Add a corpus-size gate: below ~200K tokens, bypass retrieval entirely and cache the whole corpus in the prompt, which also composes with the caching component.

techniques.name: Complexity-aware execution routing with escalation (Adaptive-RAG + Self-Route)
techniques.description: Stage 0 of the pipeline. (1) A cheap router (a 60M-770M fine-tuned classifier, or a single short LLM call returning a label) assigns the incoming task prompt one of at least four plans: NO_RETRIEVAL (answer from parametric knowledge or pure reasoning), SINGLE_STEP (one hybrid retrieval, rerank, compress, generate), MULTI_STEP (IRCoT loop with per-step retrieval), GLOBAL (RAPTOR/GraphRAG community-summary map-reduce or long-context escalation). (2) The plan runs with an explicit abstention output ('unanswerable from provided context'). (3) On abstention or low verifier score, escalate to the next more expensive plan (SINGLE_STEP -> MULTI_STEP -> GLOBAL/long-context), never downward. (4) Log (query features, plan chosen, success, cost) to retrain the router from production traces. Router labels are bootstrapped exactly as Adaptive-RAG does: run all plans on a sample, label each query with the cheapest plan that answered correctly.
source_titles: Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach (Self-Route)
Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
Modular RAG: Transforming RAG Systems into LEGO-like Reconfigurable Frameworks
techniques.when_to_use: Always, as the entry point of any pipeline that must serve heterogeneous tasks; essential when traffic mixes trivial lookups with multi-hop or corpus-wide questions, and whenever cost or latency SLOs exist.
techniques.tradeoffs: Adds one cheap call (~10-50 ms classifier or ~200 ms LLM label). Misrouting to a plan that is too cheap costs an escalation round trip; misrouting too expensive wastes tokens. Adaptive-RAG with GPT-3.5 reached F1 50.91 at 1.46x single-step latency vs multi-step at 3.33x; Self-Route cut tokens 39-65% at within 2.2% of long-context quality. Router drift must be monitored.
techniques.default_parameters: Router: T5-large or smaller (Adaptive-RAG found 60M-770M within ~1 F1); expect roughly 9% NO / 53% SINGLE / 38% MULTI on open-domain QA and recalibrate per domain. Self-Route: k=5 chunks of ~300 words for the cheap RAG pass; expect 57-82% of queries to be answered without escalation. Maximum escalation depth 2; hard timeout per plan. Corpus-size gate: if total corpus < ~200K tokens, route everything to cached long-context (Anthropic).

techniques.name: Query transformation fan-out with RRF fusion (rewrite, multi-query, step-back, HyDE)
techniques.description: Before retrieval, one LLM call (or a distilled rewriter) emits a structured set of retrieval queries from the task prompt: (a) a search-friendly rewrite of the literal question (Rewrite-Retrieve-Read); (b) 2-4 paraphrases or decomposed sub-queries (multi-query); (c) a step-back abstraction to the governing principle/standard (Step-Back); (d) optionally a hypothetical answer passage to embed (HyDE). Each variant is run through the hybrid retriever in parallel; result lists are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion score(d) = sum 1/(k + rank_i(d)), k=60, then deduplicated and passed to the reranker. Variant generation is a schema-constrained JSON output so the stage is deterministic to parse and easy to disable per variant.
source_titles: Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)
Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods
techniques.when_to_use: When user phrasing differs from document vocabulary (plain-English questions over formal specs/code), when questions are underspecified or multi-faceted, and when recall at the top of the ranking is the measured bottleneck (Barnett FP2).
techniques.tradeoffs: One extra LLM call (~0.5-1 s) plus N parallel retrievals (cheap). HyDE can inject hallucinated detail when the model lacks domain knowledge (private identifiers); step-back can over-generalize for very specific lookups. Gains: Step-Back +7 to +27 points on PaLM-2L across MMLU Physics/Chemistry, TimeQA, MuSiQue; HyDE matches fine-tuned retrievers zero-shot; Rewrite-Retrieve-Read gives consistent gains on HotpotQA/AmbigNQ/PopQA/MMLU.
techniques.default_parameters: 3-5 total query variants (1 rewrite, 2-3 multi-query/sub-queries, 1 step-back; HyDE only when a domain-knowledge flag is set). RRF k=60 (Cormack et al.), equal retriever weights. Retrieve top-50 per variant, fuse, keep top-150 for reranking. Temperature 0 for the rewrite call; cache rewrites by normalized query hash.

techniques.name: Contextualized hybrid retrieval with rerank cascade
techniques.description: Indexing: split documents into structure-aware chunks (respect headings, code blocks, table rows, requirement IDs) of ~200-800 tokens with ~10-15% overlap; for each chunk, generate a 50-100-token context sentence (what document/section it comes from, what it is about) with a cheap LLM and prepend it before computing both the dense embedding and the BM25 term index; attach metadata (doc type, system, version, date, component ID, severity). Query time: run BM25 and dense search in parallel with metadata pre-filters derived from the task prompt, fuse with RRF, take top-150, score with a cross-encoder reranker, keep top-20 (or top-10 for small-context models), and pass to compression/ordering. Index versioning: every embedding-model or chunking change triggers a full re-index behind a blue/green alias.
source_titles: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods
Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
techniques.when_to_use: Default retrieval path for every corpus larger than ~200K tokens; mandatory when exact identifiers (part numbers, error codes, requirement IDs, function names) matter, since BM25 catches what embeddings blur.
techniques.tradeoffs: Contextualization costs a one-time ~$1 per million document tokens (with prompt caching) and doubles index build time; reranking 150 candidates adds roughly 100-500 ms. Measured benefit: top-20 retrieval failures fall from 5.7% to 1.9% (-67%). Reranker depth is the main latency knob.
techniques.default_parameters: Chunk 200-800 tokens (600 with 100 overlap per GraphRAG; 'no more than a few hundred' per Anthropic), context prefix 50-100 tokens, RRF k=60, rerank depth 150 -> keep 20 (Anthropic found top-20 > top-10 > top-5), cap at 20 because reader performance saturates there (Liu et al.). Re-index on any embedding/chunking change (Barnett).

techniques.name: Corrective evidence gating with reflection signals (CRAG + Self-RAG)
techniques.description: After reranking, a lightweight evaluator scores each candidate chunk for relevance to the (rewritten) query on a [-1,1] or {relevant, irrelevant} scale. Aggregate the scores into a three-way decision: CORRECT (at least one chunk above the upper threshold) -> refine by splitting chunks into 'knowledge strips' (sentences/paragraphs), re-scoring strips and keeping only relevant ones; INCORRECT (all chunks below the lower threshold) -> discard and invoke a configured fallback retriever (secondary corpus, web search, or a different index such as the RAPTOR tree) or return an honest abstention; AMBIGUOUS -> use both refined strips and fallback results. After generation, a second judge emits IsSup {fully, partially, no support} per statement and IsUse {1-5}; segments with 'no support' are filtered or regenerated (hard constraint) or down-weighted in a beam (soft, weights IsRel 1.0, IsSup 1.0, IsUse 0.5). Decide whether to retrieve at all with a Retrieve token/judge whose threshold is configurable.
source_titles: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG)
Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
RA-DIT: Retrieval-Augmented Dual Instruction Tuning
techniques.when_to_use: Whenever the corpus may lack the answer (Barnett FP1) or retrieval is noisy; critical for safety- or compliance-relevant engineering answers where an unsupported claim is worse than an abstention.
techniques.tradeoffs: Adds a small-model pass over 20 chunks (tens of ms with a 0.77B T5 or a cross-encoder) plus one judge call post-generation. Thresholds are dataset-sensitive (CRAG used (0.59,-0.99) on PopQA but (0.95,-0.91) on Biography) and must be calibrated per domain. Measured: CRAG lifts LLaMA2-7B RAG from 48.9 -> 59.5 on PubHealth and 43.4 -> 53.7 on ARC; Self-RAG 7B beats ChatGPT on PopQA (54.9 vs 29.3) and FactScore (81.2 vs 71.8).
techniques.default_parameters: Evaluator: T5-large-class (~0.77B) or cross-encoder reranker reused as scorer. Start thresholds at upper 0.5, lower -0.9 and calibrate on 100-300 labeled queries per domain. Self-RAG critique weights 1.0/1.0/0.5; retrieval trigger P(Retrieve=yes) > 0.2 (0 when citations are mandatory); beam width 2 if segment-level search is used. Fallback retriever: one configured, with a maximum of one fallback round.

techniques.name: Budgeted context compression and position-aware ordering
techniques.description: Given the gated top-k chunks and a token budget B: (1) compute question-aware chunk scores (reranker scores or small-LM conditional perplexity); (2) extractive compression: keep only the top 1-2 most relevant sentences per chunk (RECOMP extractive) or CRAG knowledge strips; abstractive compression (distilled T5-large or a cheap LLM) when sources are narrative, with the rule that the compressor may return an empty string if the evidence does not help (selective augmentation); (3) token-level compression (LLMLingua) for demonstrations/instructions, never for code or identifiers; (4) reorder so the highest-scored evidence sits at the start and the next-highest at the end of the context (counter the U-shaped position effect); (5) preserve a source-span pointer on every compressed unit so citations resolve to original text.
source_titles: RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Context Compression and Selective Augmentation
LongLLMLingua: Accelerating and Enhancing LLMs in Long Context Scenarios via Prompt Compression
LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
techniques.when_to_use: Default between retrieval and generation; most valuable when k is large, contexts exceed a few thousand tokens, per-token cost matters, or the generator is a small/chat-sized model prone to position bias.
techniques.tradeoffs: RECOMP keeps 5-10% of tokens at <=~10% relative loss (NQ EM 39.39 -> 37.04 with 660 -> 36 tokens); LongLLMLingua gains +21.4% on NQ with ~4x fewer tokens and 1.4-2.6x latency speedup. Abstractive compression lowers citation recall (ALCE SUMM: 73.6 -> 68.9) and risks paraphrase errors on numbers; extractive is safer for specs and code.
techniques.default_parameters: Budget B = 2,000-4,000 tokens of evidence for chat-sized models (RAPTOR used a 2,000-token collapsed-tree budget ~ top-20 nodes). Extractive: top-1 sentence per chunk for single-hop, top-2 for multi-hop (RECOMP). Compression ratio 2x-6x for prose (LongLLMLingua), 1x (none) for code/tables. Ordering: best-first, second-best-last, remainder in the middle. Empty-evidence passthrough enabled.

techniques.name: Iterative retrieval loop for multi-hop and long-form tasks (IRCoT + FLARE)
techniques.description: For MULTI_STEP plans: initialize context with the fused top chunks; loop up to S steps: generate one reasoning step (CoT sentence or sub-answer); if the step contains low-confidence tokens (logprob below tau) or an explicit 'need more info' marker, use the step text (or a generated sub-question) as a new retrieval query, retrieve top-k, dedupe into context, and regenerate the step; stop when the model emits a final answer or the step budget is exhausted. For long-form generation (reports, postmortems), apply the same loop per paragraph/section (FLARE) rather than per reasoning step. Each hop is logged with its query, retrieved IDs and confidence for traceability.
source_titles: Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions (IRCoT)
Active Retrieval Augmented Generation (FLARE)
Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
techniques.when_to_use: Questions needing evidence from multiple documents/components (trace a requirement to tests to incidents), root-cause analysis across logs, and long-form synthesis where information needs emerge during writing.
techniques.tradeoffs: Latency and cost scale with hops: Adaptive-RAG's multi-step averaged 2.1-4.7 retrieval rounds and 3.3-8.8x single-step time. Gains: IRCoT +21 points retrieval and +15 points QA on HotpotQA/2Wiki/MuSiQue/IIRC. Risk of query drift and runaway loops without a budget.
techniques.default_parameters: Max steps S=4 (observed averages 2-5); k=4-8 new chunks per hop with dedupe; FLARE confidence threshold tau on min token probability around 0.4-0.8 (tune on validation; lower tau retrieves less); stop on a final-answer marker; total token budget enforced across hops.

techniques.name: Hierarchical and graph indexing for document- and corpus-level questions (RAPTOR + GraphRAG)
techniques.description: Build two auxiliary indexes alongside chunk vectors. RAPTOR tree: leaf chunks ~100 tokens; embed; reduce with UMAP; cluster with GMM (BIC-selected cluster count, soft membership); summarize each cluster with a cheap LLM; recurse until one root; store every node in the vector index with a level tag; query with the collapsed-tree strategy (search all levels, take nodes by score within a 2,000-token budget). GraphRAG: extract entities/relations per 600-token chunk with 1-2 gleaning passes; build a graph; Leiden community detection to produce hierarchical communities C0 (root) to C3; pre-generate community reports; answer GLOBAL plan queries by map (score each community report's partial answer) and reduce (synthesize top partial answers). The router sends 'what are the themes/risks across X' to GraphRAG, 'what does this document say about Y' to RAPTOR collapsed tree, and precise lookups to chunk retrieval.
source_titles: RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval
From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Long technical documents (specifications, standards, design docs) and corpus-wide sensemaking (patterns across incident reports, cross-cutting requirements), where chunk retrieval fails on 'general' and 'implicit whole-context' queries (Li et al.'s RAG failure categories).
techniques.tradeoffs: Indexing cost is high (LLM summarization of every cluster/community; GraphRAG entity extraction over every chunk) and must be re-run on corpus change. Query cost at C0 is 9-43x lower than source-text map-reduce. Gains: RAPTOR+GPT-4 QuALITY 82.6% vs 62.3% prior best; GraphRAG 72-83% win rate on comprehensiveness. Summaries can hallucinate; keep provenance links to leaf chunks.
techniques.default_parameters: RAPTOR: leaf chunk 100 tokens, GMM with UMAP, collapsed-tree retrieval with 2,000-token budget (~top-20 nodes). GraphRAG: 600-token chunks, 100-token overlap, 1 gleaning pass (more for recall-critical corpora), Leiden hierarchy, default query level C1/C2 (C0 for cheap overviews, C3 for detail). Rebuild incrementally per document delta.

techniques.name: Citation-grounded generation with NLI verification
techniques.description: The generation prompt requires every factual statement to carry one or more citation markers [n] referring to evidence units in context (which carry source-span pointers back through compression). Post-generation: split the answer into statements; for each statement, run an NLI/entailment judge (TRUE-style T5-11B or an LLM judge) over the concatenated cited passages; citation recall = fraction of statements entailed by their citations; citation precision = fraction of citations individually necessary (a citation is irrelevant if it does not entail the statement alone and removing it leaves the rest still entailing). Statements failing recall are regenerated with a constrained prompt or flagged/removed; precision failures prune superfluous citations. Also compute RAGAS faithfulness (statement-level support against all context) as a cheaper proxy.
source_titles: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
techniques.when_to_use: Any answer a human will act on (compliance, safety, engineering decisions) and any output that will be audited; mandatory when the pipeline feeds downstream automated steps.
techniques.tradeoffs: One NLI pass per statement (batchable, ~tens of ms each with a cross-encoder; one LLM call with a judge). Even strong models lack full citation support ~50% of the time on long-form ELI5 (ALCE), so expect regeneration overhead. Compression lowers citation recall; interactive 'check the full passage' did not help ChatGPT (ALCE INTERACT).
techniques.default_parameters: Top-5 full passages (ALCE main setting) or up to 20 compressed evidence units for GPT-4-class models; require >=1 citation per factual statement; release gate at citation recall >= 0.8 and faithfulness >= 0.9 on sampled traffic (RAGAS faithfulness agrees with humans at 0.95); maximum one regeneration round per statement.

techniques.name: Reference-free evaluation triad with calibrated judges (RAGAS + ARES + failure-point telemetry)
techniques.description: Offline: generate synthetic in-domain QA from the corpus (FLAN-T5-class or an LLM), filtered so the retriever returns the source passage at rank 1, with weak and strong negatives; fine-tune or prompt judges for context relevance, faithfulness and answer relevance; collect 150-300 human labels per domain and apply prediction-powered inference to produce confidence intervals and rank pipeline configurations. Online: sample N% of traffic, compute the RAGAS triad plus gold-in-top-k (when feedback exists), abstention rate, schema-validation failures, latency, and token cost; attribute every failure to Barnett's FP1-FP7; alert on drift; feed labeled failures back into router and retriever training. Evaluate position sensitivity by permuting gold-passage position on the validation set.
source_titles: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
techniques.when_to_use: From day one of any production deployment; 'validation is only feasible during operation' (Barnett), so offline benchmarks alone are insufficient.
techniques.tradeoffs: Judge calls add cost (sample rather than evaluate 100%); RAGAS context relevance is the least reliable metric (0.70 human agreement); ARES needs ~150 labels but yields Kendall tau 0.91-0.97 and intervals. Synthetic data can mirror the generator's biases.
techniques.default_parameters: Sample 5-10% of production traffic for judge scoring; 150-300 human labels per domain for PPI calibration (ARES); release thresholds: faithfulness >= 0.9, answer relevance >= 0.8, citation recall >= 0.8, abstention rate within an expected band; compute failure-point attribution weekly; re-run position-sensitivity test on every generator model change.

architecture_recommendations: 1. Model the component as a typed execution graph with four control-flow primitives (linear, conditional, branching+fusion, bounded loop) per Modular RAG; every published method (Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, IRCoT, RAPTOR, GraphRAG) is then a declarative sub-graph/configuration, not new code. Ship a YAML/JSON 'recipe' format and a registry of operators (rewriter, retriever, fuser, reranker, gate, compressor, generator, verifier, judge).

2. Put a planner/router at the entry: it parses the natural-language task prompt into a structured TaskSpec (intent, answer format, domain, required evidence types, cost/latency tier, citation requirement) and selects a plan among NO_RETRIEVAL, SINGLE_STEP, MULTI_STEP, GLOBAL, LONG_CONTEXT. Start with an LLM-labeled router; replace with a distilled 60M-770M classifier trained on production traces (Adaptive-RAG). Always allow explicit abstention and upward escalation (Self-Route).

3. Separate indexing from serving. Indexing pipeline: structure-aware chunking (respect headings, code blocks, tables, requirement IDs), contextual prefix generation, dual indexing (BM25 + dense), metadata schema, optional RAPTOR tree and GraphRAG communities, all versioned behind aliases so embedding/chunking changes can be blue/green re-indexed (Barnett).

4. Retrieval stage defaults: parallel BM25 + dense with metadata pre-filters, RRF k=60 fusion, rerank 150 -> 20, evidence cap aligned with the reader-saturation point (~20) and the model's context size. Make retriever adapters pluggable (vector DB, search engine, SQL/metadata store, code-symbol index, ticketing API) behind one interface returning (text, source_span, metadata, score).

5. Insert a corrective evidence gate between rerank and generation (CRAG three-way decision with calibrated thresholds, configurable fallback retriever) and a selective-augmentation compressor (RECOMP-style: may return nothing) with position-aware ordering (LongLLMLingua, Lost in the Middle). Every compressed unit must keep a pointer to its original span.

6. Generation stage: prompt templates that (a) state evidence may be irrelevant and must be ignored if so (RA-DIT lesson), (b) require per-statement citations, (c) enforce output schema (JSON/Markdown/table) with validation and one repair retry (Barnett FP5), (d) expose temperature, max evidence, and persona/domain system prompts as configuration.

7. Verification stage: statement splitting, NLI-based citation recall/precision (ALCE), Self-RAG-style IsSup/IsUse judgments with configurable soft weights or hard filters; unsupported statements are regenerated or removed; abstention when nothing is supported.

8. Observability as a first-class module: trace every request (plan, queries, retrieved IDs and ranks, gate decisions, compression ratio, tokens, latency, judge scores, citations), attribute failures to FP1-FP7, sample traffic for RAGAS/ARES scoring, and store traces as training data for router, retriever and gate recalibration.

9. Cost controls: corpus-size gate (<200K tokens -> cached whole-corpus prompt, no retrieval), step and token budgets per plan, semantic/exact caching of rewrites, retrievals and final answers keyed on normalized query + index version, and model tiering (small model for routing/gating/compression, frontier model for synthesis).

10. Domain adapters: a DomainProfile object bundles chunking rules, metadata schema, retriever weights, gate thresholds, compression policy (extractive for code/specs, abstractive for prose), citation strictness and judge prompts; engineering profiles (code, requirements, standards, test logs, incidents, CAD/BOM) are shipped as presets and overridden per deployment.

11. Agentic wrapper with governance: the planner may call retrieval operators as tools in a bounded loop (max steps, max tokens, deterministic fallbacks), writes an audit log, and can hand off to task-decomposition and verification components through the same TaskSpec/Evidence/Answer message types (Singh et al. governance gaps).

12. Evaluation harness in CI: synthetic in-domain QA generation with hard negatives, 150-300 human labels per domain for PPI calibration, regression suites for retrieval recall@k, position-sensitivity, faithfulness, citation recall/precision, abstention correctness, latency and cost per plan; block releases on threshold regressions.
pitfalls: Missing content answered anyway (Barnett FP1): the corpus lacks the answer but the model fabricates one. Mitigate with a corrective gate (CRAG INCORRECT branch), explicit abstention instructions, selective augmentation that returns no evidence (RECOMP), and abstention-rate monitoring.

Gold document ranked below top-k (Barnett FP2): mitigate with hybrid BM25+dense, contextual chunking, query fan-out with RRF, and rerank depth 150 -> 20 (Anthropic: -67% failures); measure recall@k against labeled sets.

Retrieved but lost in consolidation or ignored in the middle (Barnett FP3; Liu et al. 'Lost in the Middle'): accuracy drops from 75.8% to 53.8% when the gold passage moves from position 1 to 10. Mitigate with reranking, best-first/second-best-last ordering, compression to a budget, and capping evidence near 20 chunks.

Answer in context but not extracted (Barnett FP4): noise or contradictions distract the model. Mitigate with knowledge-strip refinement (CRAG), extractive compression, prompts that license ignoring irrelevant text, and RA-DIT-style fine-tuning when weights are available.
Wrong output format (Barnett FP5): mitigate with schema-constrained generation, validators and one repair retry.
Incorrect specificity and incomplete answers (Barnett FP6/FP7): mitigate with TaskSpec capturing the required granularity, completeness judges, and multi-step plans for multi-part questions.

Over-retrieval and over-compute on simple queries (Adaptive-RAG; Self-RAG motivation): fixed k retrieval for every query wastes cost and can hurt accuracy (no-retrieval beat single-step on GPT-3.5 F1). Mitigate with complexity routing and a retrieval trigger threshold.

RAG failure categories under long-context comparison (Li et al. 2024): multi-step reasoning, general queries, long/complex queries, implicit whole-context queries. Mitigate with IRCoT loops, GraphRAG/RAPTOR for global queries, and Self-Route escalation to long context.
Compression trades citation recall for correctness (ALCE SUMM/SNIPPET: citation recall 73.6 -> 68.9/65.3): keep source-span pointers and prefer extractive compression when citations are mandatory.
Incomplete citation support even in strong models (ALCE: best models lack full support ~50% on ELI5): verify with NLI and regenerate; never trust self-reported citations.
Hallucinated hypothetical documents in HyDE and over-abstraction in Step-Back for domain-private entities: gate these transforms behind a domain-knowledge flag and measure their marginal recall.
Hard-coded thresholds that do not transfer (CRAG thresholds vary from (0.59,-0.99) to (0.95,-0.91) across datasets): calibrate per domain on a labeled set and re-calibrate on model change.

Unreliable automatic judges, especially context relevance (RAGAS 0.70 human agreement) and uncalibrated LLM scores: use ARES-style fine-tuned judges with PPI and human-labeled validation sets; treat scores comparatively.
Expensive index rebuilds and silent staleness (Barnett; GraphRAG/RAPTOR indexing cost): version indexes, rebuild incrementally, and expose index version in every trace and cache key.
Runaway agentic loops and ungoverned autonomy (Singh et al.): enforce step/token budgets, deterministic fallbacks and audit logs.
Validation only feasible in operation (Barnett): do not ship on offline benchmarks alone; sample live traffic for judge scoring and human review from day one.
evaluation_metrics: Retrieval: recall@k and gold-in-top-k (k=5,10,20), MRR/nDCG@10 against labeled or synthetic query-passage pairs; retrieval failure rate at top-20 (Anthropic reports 5.7% -> 1.9%)
Post-consolidation gold-in-context rate (Barnett FP3) and context relevance (RAGAS: fraction of context sentences needed)
Faithfulness / groundedness (RAGAS statement-level support; 0.95 human agreement), answer faithfulness (ARES judge with PPI confidence intervals)
Answer relevance (RAGAS question-regeneration cosine; ARES judge) and task correctness (EM/F1/accuracy on domain QA sets; FactScore-style for long-form)
Citation recall and citation precision via NLI (ALCE/TRUE), plus fraction of statements with at least one citation
Abstention metrics: abstention rate, abstention precision (correctly declined unanswerable) and recall (missed unanswerables), Self-Route 'unanswerable' fraction
Routing metrics: plan distribution, escalation rate, router accuracy against cheapest-successful-plan labels, cost per plan
Efficiency: end-to-end latency p50/p95, tokens per query (input/output), compression ratio, relative time vs single-step (Adaptive-RAG style), cost per 1,000 queries
Position-sensitivity test: accuracy as a function of gold-passage position (U-shape magnitude, Liu et al.)
Format compliance: schema validation pass rate and repair-retry rate (FP5)
Completeness and specificity judges (FP6/FP7) on sampled traffic; human preference win rates for comprehensiveness/diversity on global questions (GraphRAG protocol)
Failure-point attribution distribution (FP1-FP7) over time as a drift and regression signal; judge-human agreement (Kendall tau, pairwise accuracy) re-measured per domain
engineering_adaptation_notes: Code: chunk by syntactic unit (function/class/module) with a contextual prefix naming file path, module and purpose; index symbols and identifiers with BM25 (exact match matters more than semantics); use extractive compression only (never token-dropping on code); add a code-symbol index (LSP/ctags) as an additional retriever fused via RRF; verify claims by compiling/running or by NLI against the exact span.

Specifications and standards: long, hierarchical documents suit RAPTOR trees seeded by heading structure; retain clause/section IDs as metadata and in the contextual prefix; step-back queries map naturally to 'which clause/principle governs this'; citations must resolve to clause numbers and revision/version.

Requirements and traceability: store requirement ID, parent/child links, verification method and status as metadata; multi-step IRCoT plans implement trace queries (requirement -> design -> test -> incident); GraphRAG entity graphs can be built directly from existing traceability links instead of LLM extraction, cutting indexing cost.

Test logs and telemetry: high-volume, repetitive, structured text; pre-aggregate (dedupe stack traces, cluster failures) before indexing; BM25 on error codes dominates; time-window metadata filters are essential; compression should be extractive and preserve numbers and timestamps exactly.

Incident reports and postmortems: narrative sources where abstractive compression and GraphRAG community summaries (themes, recurring root causes across incidents) add value; global plan for 'what patterns recur', single-step for 'what happened in INC-1234'; completeness judges matter because postmortems are multi-part.

CAD/BOM metadata: mostly tabular; route to structured/SQL retrieval tools with the LLM generating filters rather than embeddings over flattened rows; embed only descriptive fields; fuse structured results with document chunks through the same Evidence interface; citation = row/part ID and revision.

Domain profiles should set: chunk policy, metadata schema, retriever weights (lexical heavier for identifiers), gate thresholds calibrated on 100-300 labeled queries, compression mode, citation strictness, judge prompts, and the corpus-size gate for whole-corpus caching of small manuals or standards.

Security and governance: metadata-level access control enforced at retrieval (pre-filter), PII/secret redaction before indexing, audit logs of evidence used per answer, and versioned indexes so an answer can be reproduced against the index snapshot it used.
composition_notes: Hybrid retrieval: Pipeline RAG is the orchestrator and hybrid retrieval is its retrieval operator; this dossier's defaults (contextual chunking, BM25+dense, RRF k=60, rerank 150 -> 20) define the contract the hybrid retrieval component must honor, and the query fan-out stage supplies it multiple queries plus metadata filters. The retrieval component owns index versioning; the pipeline owns the corpus-size gate and the decision to call it at all.

Task decomposition: the router's MULTI_STEP plan and IRCoT loop are where decomposition plugs in; the decomposition component turns a complex prompt into sub-questions, each executed as one retrieve-and-reason hop, and its DAG also drives the parallel branches of a GraphRAG map step. Step-back abstraction is a decomposition primitive (specific -> principle) shared between the two components.

Answer verification: Self-RAG IsSup/IsUse judgments, CRAG evidence scoring, ALCE citation precision/recall and the RAGAS/ARES triad are the verification component's inputs and outputs; the pipeline exposes statements, citations and source spans so verification can run NLI, and consumes verification results to regenerate, filter or abstain (self-consistency style multi-sample verification composes at the generation stage).

Parallelization: query variants, per-retriever searches, per-chunk evaluator scoring, REPLUG-style parallel generations over evidence subsets, and GraphRAG map steps over community reports are all embarrassingly parallel fan-out/fan-in points; the parallelization component should provide a bounded fan-out primitive with fusion (RRF or score aggregation) and a global token/latency budget.

Caching: cache rewrites by normalized query, retrieval results by (query variant, index version, filters), contextual prefixes and summaries by chunk hash, and final answers by semantic similarity with an index-version check; prompt caching of a whole corpus under ~200K tokens replaces retrieval entirely (Anthropic: >2x latency and up to 90% cost reduction) and is the cheapest plan the router can select.

Prompting and architecture best practices: use structured outputs for router/rewriter/judge stages, instruct the generator that evidence may be irrelevant, place instructions and the best evidence at the context edges (Lost in the Middle), keep system prompts and domain profiles cacheable prefixes, bound agentic loops with explicit budgets, and run offline+online evaluation with calibrated judges so every configuration change is measured against the failure-point taxonomy.
